findings.paper_title: F.789 Annex D - Reserves and General Balances 2025 26
findings.headline: General Fund Balance remains at approximately £1.0m, providing only 1-2 weeks of operational cover.
findings.detail: The General Fund Balance (B8000) is £1,014,754 at April 2025 and £1,015,236 from April 2026 onwards, remaining static. For a district council, this represents extremely tight unallocated reserves.
findings.matters: A general fund balance of £1m is insufficient to absorb service disruption, demand spikes, or delayed income. This leaves the council vulnerable to any unexpected expenditure and dependent on its earmarked reserves.
findings.figures: General Fund Balance: £1,014,754 (April 2025) → £1,015,236 (April 2026 onwards)

findings.paper_title: F.789 Annex D - Reserves and General Balances 2025 26
findings.headline: New District Council Initiatives reserve of £1.0m created in 2025/26, representing a significant new commitment or spending priority.
findings.detail: RES296 District Council Initiatives is established with zero opening balance at April 2025 but allocated £1,038,670 in the 2025/26 budget year, growing to £529,920 by forecast April 2027. This is a substantial new reserve creation in a single year with no prior commitment.
findings.matters: A large reserve created in one year without prior provision suggests either new discretionary spending, new statutory obligations, or a strategic reallocation that lenders should understand in the context of the council's stated financial priorities.
findings.figures: District Council Initiatives: £0 (April 2025) → £1,038,670 (budgeted 2025/26) → £529,920 (April 2027)
findings.quote: RES296 District Council Initiatives

findings.paper_title: F.789 Annex D - Reserves and General Balances 2025 26
findings.headline: Council is drawing on Future Deficits Reserve, suggesting anticipated budget shortfalls.
findings.detail: The Future Deficits Reserve (RES229) has been reduced from £1,212,037 at April 2025 to £874,957 by April 2026. This reserve exists specifically to cover budget deficits from government funding reductions. The drawdown indicates the council has already used part of this buffer.
findings.matters: Depletion of a deficit-specific reserve demonstrates the council has already faced or is planning for funding gaps that could not be met from normal operations.
findings.figures: Future Deficits Reserve: £1,212,037 (April 2025) → £874,957 (April 2026)
findings.quote: RES229 Future Deficits Reserve To fund any budget deficits resulting in the reduction of funding from the Government.

findings.paper_title: F.789 Annex D - Reserves and General Balances 2025 26
findings.headline: Total earmarked reserves forecast to decline by £2.2m (17%) in 2026/27, from £12.4m to £10.2m.
findings.detail: Earmarked reserves move from £12,494,468 at April 2025 to £12,353,492 (revised) at April 2026, then decline significantly to £10,202,032 forecast by April 2027. This represents a planned substantial drawdown of reserves in a single year.
findings.matters: Sustained reserve depletion at this rate indicates the council may be using reserves to fund recurring expenditure rather than one-time costs, signalling underlying structural budget pressure.
findings.figures: Total Earmarked Reserves: £12,494,468 (April 2025) → £12,353,492 (April 2026) → £10,202,032 (April 2027)

findings.paper_title: F.789 Annex D - Reserves and General Balances 2025 26
findings.headline: Capital Receipts Reserve of £3.4m will be fully consumed in 2025/26, leaving no capital receipts buffer for future years.
findings.detail: The Capital Receipts Reserve stands at £3,365,831 (revised April 2026) and is forecast to reduce to zero by April 2027. This reserve funds capital expenditure from one-time asset sales and cannot be replenished. Once exhausted, the council will be entirely dependent on borrowing for future capital needs.
findings.matters: Capital receipts are non-renewable. Exhausting this leaves no buffer for emergency capital expenditure and increases reliance on borrowing, which raises council debt servicing costs and constrains fiscal flexibility.
findings.figures: Capital Receipts Reserve: £3,155,997 (April 2025) → £3,365,831 (April 2026) → £0 (April 2027)
findings.quote: B8700 Capital Receipts Reserve To fund general fund capital expenditure

findings.headline: Built Environment sector overspent by £245,007 (30.4%), the largest sectoral overspend, driven by cemetery and parks costs.
findings.detail: The Built Environment directorate (containing cemeteries, parks, car parks, and property services) spent £1,050,177 against a budget of £805,170. Mile End Cemetery alone overspent by £16,225 and Parks & Gardens by £14,577. This suggests unplanned maintenance, increased activity, or cost pressures across multiple inherited assets.
findings.matters: Large overspends in asset-intensive services suggest deferred maintenance is now surfacing, unexpected repairs are occurring, or volumes are higher than predicted. For a lender, this indicates the council's asset base may be consuming more revenue than anticipated.
findings.figures: Budget £805,170, actual £1,050,177, overspend £245,007

findings.headline: Household Waste costs overran by £105,588 (7.3%), indicating sustained service price or volume pressure.
findings.detail: Household Waste (WST001) cost £1,559,298 against a budget of £1,453,710. This is a material pressure across a core council service and suggests either waste volumes have grown, contractor costs have risen, or disposal costs have increased. It sits within the overall Finance directorate overspend.
findings.matters: Waste costs are a substantial and generally inelastic council expense. An overspend here that cannot be recovered suggests the council's cost base is growing faster than anticipated and reducing budget headroom for other priorities.
findings.figures: Budgeted £1,453,710, actual £1,559,298, overspend £105,588

findings.headline: Council Tax Collection spent £82,917 more (51.5%) than budgeted, suggesting collection difficulties or resource constraints.
findings.detail: Council Tax Collection (LTC001) cost £244,107 against a budget of £161,190. This more-than-doubling of collection costs is unusual and could indicate staffing pressures, higher bad debts requiring recovery effort, or system investments. It is the third-largest individual overspend.
findings.matters: Rising collection costs that are not anticipated indicate either collection rates are falling (meaning lower income to the council) or the council is having to spend more to collect what it budgeted for. Either signals cash-flow risk.
findings.figures: Budgeted £161,190, actual £244,107, overspend £82,917
findings.quote: LTC001 Council Tax Collection 129,950 161,190 244,107 82,917

findings.headline: Legal Services overspent by £96,227 (23.8%), a material increase in professional costs.
findings.detail: Legal (SUP004) spent £499,317 against a budget of £403,090. This is the second-largest overspend and suggests either unplanned legal work, employment disputes, or governance matters requiring external counsel. The council absorbed this as a significant cost pressure.
findings.matters: A large legal overspend can signal underlying governance issues, employment disputes, regulatory challenges, or restructuring. Lenders care because legal costs that are not forecast are a warning sign of operational turbulence.
findings.figures: Budgeted £403,090, actual £499,317, overspend £96,227

findings.headline: Rent Allowances overspent by £178,712 (23.6%), driven by higher housing support demand or benefit levels.
findings.detail: Housing Benefits Payments (HBP001) ran to £936,552 against a budget of £757,840. This is the largest single overspend in the outturn and indicates sustained pressure on housing support spending. The council had to accommodate a significant uplift in welfare costs.
findings.matters: Growing housing benefit claims or escalating benefit levels signal economic stress in the local population and demand for social support. For a lender, this is a leading indicator of local economic difficulty and constrained council finances.
findings.figures: Budgeted £757,840, actual £936,552, overspend £178,712

findings.paper_title: F.782 ANNEX A FINAL FoDDC Internal Audit Annual Opinion 202526
findings.headline: 13 open agreed actions from audits, including 4 Priority 1 actions requiring immediate correction
findings.detail: Five agreed actions from 2024/25 remain open, and 8 from 2025/26, for a total of 13 open agreed actions. Of these, 4 are Priority 1 (immediate corrective action required), suggesting the council is not promptly remediating identified audit findings.
findings.matters: A significant number of overdue agreed actions, particularly Priority 1 items, indicates the council is not promptly addressing control weaknesses, which leaves ongoing operational and compliance risk unresolved.
findings.figures: 5 open from 2024/25 + 8 open from 2025/26 = 13 total; 4 Priority 1, 4 Priority 2, 7 Priority 3 in 2025/26
findings.quote: Five agreed actions from 2024/25 remain open, and 8 remain open from 2025/26.

findings.paper_title: F.782 ANNEX A FINAL FoDDC Internal Audit Annual Opinion 202526
findings.headline: Leisure service provider non-compliance not being reported to the council as contractually required
findings.detail: Health and safety compliance failures at leisure facilities were not reported to FoDDC by the service provider, despite contractual requirements. This indicates a breakdown in the council's oversight and contract management of its leisure provider.
findings.matters: Non-reporting of contractually-required compliance failures represents both a control weakness and potential liability exposure, signalling gaps in the council's oversight of key service providers.
findings.figures: Leisure audit identified as significant risk; selected health and safety non-compliances not reported
findings.quote: A review of selected health and safety compliance areas identified non-compliances that had not been reported to the Council.

findings.paper_title: F.782 ANNEX A FINAL FoDDC Internal Audit Annual Opinion 202526
findings.headline: Significant control weakness: data not retained per statutory requirements or best practice
findings.detail: The Data Retention Policy and Schedule required updating. Data was not being retained in accordance with Publica's retention schedule, statutory requirements, or best practice. Although management completed agreed actions, this represents a material governance failure in compliance obligations.
findings.matters: Non-compliance with data retention and protection requirements is a regulatory risk and suggests broader control weaknesses in how the organisation manages compliance obligations.
findings.figures: Data Retention audit identified as significant risk requiring corrective action
findings.quote: Data was not retained in accordance with Publica's retention schedule, or best practice and statutory requirements.

findings.paper_title: F.782 ANNEX A FINAL FoDDC Internal Audit Annual Opinion 202526
findings.headline: Reasonable overall assurance opinion rather than substantial, indicating identified control gaps
findings.detail: The council received a Reasonable Assurance opinion for 2025/26, meaning there is a generally sound system in place but with identified issues and scope for improvement. This sits below Substantial Assurance, indicating that while controls exist, they have material weaknesses.
findings.matters: A Reasonable rather than Substantial assurance opinion directly signals that the council's control environment has identified gaps that could affect achievement of objectives, which is material to lenders assessing control risk and financial stability.
findings.figures: Reasonable Assurance for overall 2025/26; 8 Substantial assurance audits, 2 Reasonable, 1 Limited
findings.quote: On the balance of our 2025/26 audit work for Forest of Dean District Council, enhanced by the work of external agencies, I am able to offer a Reasonable Assurance opinion in respect of the areas reviewed during the year.

findings.headline: Waste vehicle fleet replacement programme of £4.9m in 2026/27 is funded entirely from capital receipts
findings.detail: A waste vehicle replacement programme of £4.9m in 2026/27 represents a substantial one-year procurement, funded wholly from capital receipts. This contrasts with prior years' waste vehicle budgets of £370k-£754k, suggesting a one-off major fleet renewal.
findings.matters: Funding from capital receipts (asset sales) creates dependency on the council's ability to sell assets; if sales do not occur as planned, the council may face a funding shortfall
findings.figures: £4,933,600 (waste vehicles 2026/27); funded by capital receipts £4,933,600
findings.quote: Replacement Vehicles Waste Vehicles 370,800             4,933,600           593,800              651,800              753,800

findings.headline: Capital programme budget increases five-fold from £3.8m in 2025/26 to £19.4m in 2026/27
findings.detail: The total capital programme jumps from £3.8m to £19.4m between the two years, driven primarily by the Five Acres project and waste vehicle replacement programme. The following year drops back to £3.9m, showing the 2026/27 spike is concentrated.
findings.matters: A five-fold increase indicates major capital intensity in one year, with implications for cash flow, borrowing needs, and financial resilience

findings.headline: Council plans internal or external borrowing of £3.9m in 2026/27 to finance capital schemes
findings.detail: The capital programme financing table specifies borrowing of £3.9m in 2026/27 and £2m in 2027/28. This represents new debt issuance primarily for the Five Acres project, with debt service obligations in future years.
findings.matters: New borrowing increases the council's debt position and future revenue costs, reducing available borrowing capacity and affecting the council's financial flexibility
findings.quote: Internal / External Borrowing -                    3,890,100           2,000,000

findings.headline: Five Acres project budget increases to £12.7m in 2026/27, representing two-thirds of the capital programme and requiring government grants and council borrowing
findings.detail: The Five Acres leisure, education and business facilities scheme budget rises significantly from £810k in 2025/26 to £12.7m in 2026/27. The financing is structured as government Levelling Up grant of £6.5m and internal/external borrowing of £3.9m, indicating a substantial new capital commitment.
findings.matters: This major capital scheme and associated borrowing increases the council's debt position, revenue commitments, and has material implications for financial resilience
findings.figures: Budget £12,734,480 (2026/27); financed by government grant £6,544,380 and borrowing £3,890,100
findings.quote: Five Acres Provision of Leisure, Education & Business Facilities 810,400             12,734,480

findings.paper_title: F.768 Annex E - Reserves and General Balances 2026 - 27 - FEB
findings.headline: Department of Works and Pensions New Burdens funding ends with no balance remaining
findings.detail: The New Burdens Funding reserve, established from government grant to cover additional Housing Benefits work from legislative changes, is projected to reach zero by April 2027 with no carry-forward.
findings.matters: This signals the end of a time-limited funding stream for statutory work; the council will need to fund ongoing Housing Benefits pressure from base revenue budget unless government restores the grant.
findings.figures: Balance 1st April 2025: (627,470); projected Balance 1st April 2027: 0
findings.quote: RES239 New Burdens Funding Funding from the Department of Works and Pensions to cover additional works following legislative changes in Housing Benefits (627,470) 38,120 16,850 572,500 0 0

findings.paper_title: F.768 Annex E - Reserves and General Balances 2026 - 27 - FEB
findings.headline: Business Rates Equalisation Reserve projected to release £470,080 in 2026-27
findings.detail: The Business Rates Retention Equalisation Reserve, the council's largest reserve at £2,575,409 in April 2026, is budgeted to have £470,080 drawn from it in 2026-27 to offset business rates income volatility.
findings.matters: Projected draws from the business rates reserve indicate expected volatility in this income stream and reliance on reserves to smooth what should be operational cashflow.
findings.figures: Balance 1st April 2026: (2,575,409); projected Balance 1st April 2027: (2,105,329)
findings.quote: RES254 BRR Equalisation Reserve To fund fluctuations in income from retained business rates (2,352,849) (222,560) (2,575,409) 470,080 (2,105,329)

findings.paper_title: F.768 Annex E - Reserves and General Balances 2026 - 27 - FEB
findings.headline: Investment Interest Reserve completely eliminated, losing £302,000 buffer
findings.detail: The Investment Interest Reserve, held to smooth fluctuations in interest rate income, has been fully depleted to £0. This reserve of £302,000 is no longer available to absorb changes in investment returns.
findings.matters: Loss of this buffer reduces the council's flexibility to manage interest income volatility and may force budget reductions if investment income falls short of projection.
findings.figures: Balance 1st April 2025: (302,000); Balance 1st April 2026: 0
findings.quote: RES293 Investment Interest To fund fluctuations in interest rates (302,000) 302,000 0 0

findings.paper_title: F.768 Annex E - Reserves and General Balances 2026 - 27 - FEB
findings.headline: Future Deficits Reserve drawn down by £387,010 to absorb government funding reductions
findings.detail: The reserve held specifically to cover budget deficits from government funding cuts fell from £1,212,037 to £825,027 in 2025-26. The council has used reserves to manage central government funding pressure rather than cutting services or borrowing.
findings.matters: Reserve depletion to fund operations signals structural financial pressure that cannot be sustained once reserves are exhausted; a lender will assess whether the council has a plan for when this reserve runs out.
findings.figures: Balance 1st April 2025: (1,212,037); Balance 1st April 2026: (825,027); decrease of £387,010
findings.quote: RES229 Future Deficits Reserve To fund any budget deficits resulting in the reduction of funding from the Government. (1,212,037) 52,840 334,170 (825,027)

findings.paper_title: F.768 Annex E - Reserves and General Balances 2026 - 27 - FEB
findings.headline: General capital reserve depleted from £920,752 to £752 in one year
findings.detail: The Capital Reserve (RES211), held to finance general fund capital expenditure, is projected to drop from £920,752 at April 2026 to just £752 by April 2027. This represents a draw of £920,000 and leaves the council with virtually no internal capital funding capacity.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand the council's unrestricted capital resilience; exhaustion of this reserve signals the council will have to borrow or seek external funding for any capital needs beyond 2027.
findings.figures: Balance 1st April 2026: (920,752); Balance 1st April 2027: (752)
findings.quote: RES211 Capital Reserve Used to finance capital expenditure. (840,752) (80,000) (920,752) (80,000) 1,000,000 (752)

findings.headline: Council tax at maximum government threshold (£6.34 per annum) to avoid referendum, indicating fiscal constraint
findings.detail: The S151 officer recommends the specific increase of £6.34 per annum because it represents the maximum threshold to avoid triggering a referendum. Council tax requirement represents 51.3% of net revenue expenditure, indicating higher grant dependency.
findings.matters: Council is using all available fiscal levers to balance budget, indicating limited flexibility to fund additional pressures.
findings.figures: Council tax increase £6.34 per annum; council tax requirement ratio 51.3% (2025-26), projected 52.0% (2026-27)
findings.quote: I recommend a council tax increase of £6.34 per annum as this will avoid the requirement for a referendum for council tax increases over the government cap.

findings.headline: General inflation not provided in budgets unless specifically flagged, creating in-year budget exposure
findings.detail: The S151 officer acknowledges general inflation has 'not been provided for unless the relevant professional officer has indicated that there are inflationary pressures.' This 'could lead to insufficient budget to maintain service levels' and in-year increases will need to be managed.
findings.matters: Budget is exposed to in-year cost pressures if inflation emerges; council will need to manage within existing allocations or use reserves.
findings.figures: Pay award 3.5% for 2026/27, then 2% from 2027/28; general inflation unbudgeted
findings.quote: In line with previous practice, general inflation has not been provided for unless the relevant professional officer has indicated that there are inflationary pressures. Whilst this creates natural efficiency savings it could lead to insufficient budget to maintain service levels.

findings.headline: Confirmed government funding reduction over next three years forcing shift to commercial property income strategy
findings.detail: The S151 officer notes confirmed funding reduction over three years and states this places 'more onus on the Council to generate more of its own income through its property and assets portfolio.' Council pursuing development of Cinderford Northern Quarter and 5 Acres sites.
findings.matters: Council's future sustainability increasingly dependent on successful property development and commercial returns; introduces execution risk into revenue forecasting.
findings.figures: 3-year confirmed funding reduction; identified property sites: Cinderford Northern Quarter and 5 Acres
findings.quote: A confirmed reduction in Government funding over the next 3 years places more onus on the Council to generate more of its own income through its property and assets portfolio.

findings.headline: Majority of 2026/27 savings proposals underway with identified slippage on achievement
findings.detail: The S151 officer acknowledges savings proposals have 'where slippage has been identified achievement has been delayed.' The council has made provision for slippage within working balances, indicating past experience of savings not materializing on schedule.
findings.matters: Indicates budgeted savings are not delivering as planned, forcing reliance on reserves to cover shortfalls; suggests cost control execution risk.
findings.figures: Provision for slippage made within working balances
findings.quote: The majority of savings proposals for 2026/2027 are being worked upon already and where slippage has been identified achievement has been delayed.

findings.headline: Future deficits reserve projected to be fully exhausted by end of 2028/29
findings.detail: The reserve created to secure the council against short-term challenges will be depleted within three years. No other dedicated contingency reserves identified to replace it.
findings.matters: Loss of contingency buffer leaves the council more vulnerable to unexpected expenditure shocks once the reserve is exhausted; reduces financial resilience during reorganisation.
findings.figures: Future deficits reserve exhausted 2028/29
findings.quote: Whilst this reserve was created to secure the Council against short-term challenges, the Council needs to recognise that this reserve is projected to be exhausted in 2028/29.

findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation in April 2028 creates structural uncertainty for multi-year planning
findings.detail: The S151 officer flags ongoing uncertainty around the Local Government Finance Settlement and the future of the Council following the White Paper on Local Government Reorganisation and Devolution. Financial settlement confirmed only to 2028/29, and medium-term funding strategy depends on reorganisation outcome.
findings.matters: Structural uncertainty directly affects the council's strategic financial planning and long-term viability as a lending risk.
findings.figures: April 2028 (reorganisation date); settlement confirmed to 2028/29
findings.quote: The on-going uncertainty around the Local Government Finance Settlement and the future of the Council following the publication of the White Paper around Local Government Reorganisation and Devolution.

findings.headline: Fees and charges maximisation is the single largest savings line at £494,740
findings.detail: The council is relying on maximising fees and charges for £494,740 of its total plan across the five years (£94,740 in 2026-27, then £100,000 per year thereafter). This is revenue-dependent, requiring either fee increases, higher service uptake, or both.
findings.matters: Income-dependent savings are more volatile than cost cuts. If demand falls, fee resistance emerges, or the council cannot increase charges, these savings will not materialise, leaving a funding gap. This is the largest single item in the plan.

findings.headline: Pension lump sum prepayment growing to £233,000, counted as a saving
findings.detail: The council plans pension lump sum prepayments of £26,000 (2026-27), £78,000 (2027-28), £129,000 (2028-29), and £233,000 (2029-30). These are classified as savings but represent a treasury/financial management decision (and potential use of borrowing) rather than service efficiency or revenue growth.
findings.matters: Pension prepayments typically use cash or borrowing capacity and affect treasury strategy. A lender would need to understand whether this is borrowing-funded and what debt implications it carries for the council's sustainability.
findings.quote: Pension Lump Sum Prepayment 26,000 78,000 129,000 233,000

findings.headline: Annual savings requirement declines sharply from £500,740 to £155,000 over the planning period
findings.detail: The council's identified savings decline significantly, from £500,740 in 2026-27 to £155,000 by 2030-31. This suggests either that early-year savings are the hardest to achieve and later ones easier, or that the council faces diminishing savings opportunities in outer years.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand whether the council retains savings capacity if facing unexpected funding pressures in later years. Declining savings headroom in outer years could indicate structural challenges.
findings.quote: Total Savings/Income over MTFS 500,740 438,000 324,000 165,000 155,000

findings.headline: Significant dependence on council tax increases (1.99% or £5 per annum) and taxbase growth of 1.25% to close budget gap.
findings.detail: The budget strategy assumes council tax rises by 1.99% (or £5 minimum) annually and taxbase growth of 1.25% per annum from 2027/28. The council notes taxbase growth will need to be closely monitored to ensure this is achievable. Economic slowdown or housing market weakness could undermine both assumptions.
findings.matters: Over-reliance on council tax and taxbase growth creates revenue risk; if growth falls short or residents reject increases (referendum), the funding gap widens.
findings.figures: Council tax assumption: 1.99% or £5 per annum (greater of); taxbase growth: 1.25% per annum from 2027/28; council tax income projected: £7.006m (2026/27) to £8.284m (2030/31)
findings.quote: The Council's taxbase is forecast to increase by 1.25% from 2027-2028 each year for the purposes of modelling the MTFS. Currently the Council's taxbase is continuing to grow. However, this will need to be closely monitored to ensure that the 1.25% per annum growth is achievable.

findings.headline: Savings strategy relies on multiple amber and red-flagged workstreams with delivery risk; £2.58m target required over MTFS.
findings.detail: The council identifies £2.58m in required savings, with a mix of green (on track), amber (at risk), and red (high-risk strategic targets). Red items require further planning and feasibility confirmation. Key items include Publica reductions (£330k), transformation (£250k), pension prepayment (£233k), and fees/charges increases (£494k). Many are dependent on external partners or economic conditions.
findings.matters: Amber and red items carry delivery risk; if savings fall short, the council will not close the budget gap, forcing reliance on reserves or emergency measures.
findings.quote: The savings considered red have significant risks associated with them at the time of publication of the MTFS. They are in essence high level strategic targets and require further planning and resourcing.

findings.headline: Business Rates Reset in 2026/27 with new revaluation cycle expected to trigger appeals, particularly from rural hospitality.
findings.detail: A full Business Rates Reset and revaluation occurs in 2026/27. The council administers £26m in business rates per annum. The 2026 revaluation generated a new round of appeals; the council flags that rural hospitality establishments are likely to lodge additional appeals, creating volatility in business rate income forecasts.
findings.matters: Business rates appeals can reduce council income below forecast; volatile income streams weaken budget certainty and may require in-year spending cuts.
findings.figures: Business rates administered: ~£26m per annum; council retains 40%; revaluation cycles (2021, 2023, 2026) each generated appeals
findings.quote: There has been lots of news around the Business Rates Revaluation and how this will impact businesses especially rural hospitality establishments. Therefore there are likely to be additional appeals from the 2026 revaluations from these establishments. This may have a negative impact on business rate valuations in this area.

findings.headline: Loss of Rural Services Delivery Grant and rural cost disadvantage not recognised in Fair Funding Review 2.0.
findings.detail: Rural Services Delivery Grant was removed in 2024 and not replaced; the Fair Funding Review 2.0 reduced recognition of rural cost drivers. The council highlights that low population density means higher per-household delivery costs (e.g., waste collection requires more vehicles and operatives). This structural disadvantage is not fully funded.
findings.matters: Unfunded rural cost drivers constrain the council's ability to deliver services efficiently; this is a structural, not cyclical, problem and signals ongoing pressure on margins.
findings.figures: Rural Services Delivery Grant removed 2024; Fair Funding 2.0 further reduced recognition of rural cost drivers
findings.quote: This follows the removal of Rural Services Delivery Grant funding given from 2016 until 2024. This means that the delivery of rural services are no longer covered by an additional grant. This was not amended for 2025/26 and this continues a clear move of finances from Rural Councils

findings.headline: Pension fund triennial revaluation found insufficient assets to meet current cost of members' past service benefits.
findings.detail: The March 2026 triennial revaluation of the Gloucestershire Pensions Fund, administered by County Council, determined that the fund's objective of holding sufficient assets to meet estimated current cost of providing members' past service benefits was not met at the valuation date. This may trigger higher contribution requirements.
findings.matters: Pension shortfalls typically require employer contribution increases; the council plans pension lump sum prepayment (£233k over three years) as a mitigation strategy, but this diverts funds from other services.
findings.figures: Pension lump sum prepayment savings: £26k (2026/27), £78k (2027/28), £129k (2028/29); total £233k
findings.quote: The triennial revaluation of the Fund based on the position as at 31st March 2026, found that the Fund's objective of holding sufficient assets to meet the estimated current cost of providing members' past service benefits was not met at the valuation date.

findings.headline: Council likely to cease to exist after March 2028 due to Local Government Reorganisation, creating governance and continuity risk.
findings.detail: Following a White Paper on Local Government Reorganisation, Forest of Dean is unlikely to exist after March 2028 when a new unitary council or councils takes over. An announcement confirming the future is expected in summer. This creates strategic uncertainty around financial planning and service continuity.
findings.matters: Lenders cannot assess the continuity or credit-worthiness of an entity that may cease to exist; succession arrangements and the stability of any successor body are unknown.
findings.figures: Timeline: current council operates until March 2028; 7 Gloucestershire councils to be replaced by new unitary structure
findings.quote: This means that the Council is unlikely to exist after March 2028 and a new unitary Council or Councils will take over from the 7 current Councils in Gloucestershire.

findings.headline: Future Deficits Reserve will be exhausted by end of 2027/28, eliminating the council's main buffer for forecast shortfalls.
findings.detail: The MTFS projects the Future Deficits Reserve will be depleted by end of 2027/28, covering the 2027/28 deficit only. After exhaustion, any in-year shortfalls will have no dedicated reserve to draw from, forcing the council to cut spending, increase income, or use other reserves.
findings.matters: Reserve exhaustion removes a critical buffer against unexpected costs or forecast errors; the council would then face forced service cuts or emergency borrowing.
findings.figures: Future Deficits Reserve covers 2027/28 deficit only; exhausted thereafter
findings.quote: The MTFS indicates that without action, the Future Deficits Reserve will be exhausted in 2027-2028.

findings.headline: Cumulative funding gap of £3.327m over the five-year MTFS period with accelerating deficits.
findings.detail: The council faces yearly funding gaps ranging from £508k (2027/28) to £1.411m (2029/30), totalling £3.327m cumulatively. The gap reflects reductions in government funding including the Fair Funding Review 2.0 and loss of rural services delivery grant. The strategy relies on delivering savings across multiple workstreams to bridge this.
findings.matters: A £3.327m structural deficit over five years signals the council will require sustained savings delivery or service reductions; inability to meet these targets would force reserve drawdown or borrowing.
findings.quote: The latest projections indicate a gap of £3.327m for the period of the MTFS (2026/27 to 2030/31).

findings.paper_title: F.768 Full Council Report - Revenue and Capital Budget 2026_2027
findings.headline: Capital programme will require borrowing towards end of 2026-2027 onwards, increasing debt servicing costs
findings.detail: The council's current capital programme cannot be fully financed from existing resources and will require borrowing towards the end of 2026-2027. The council notes that borrowing may be either internal or external. This will increase future revenue costs through debt servicing at a time when the council is already under revenue pressure.
findings.matters: New borrowing increases fixed costs in the revenue budget and reduces flexibility in future years when savings targets must be met; lenders need to assess whether the council's borrowing capacity is adequate.
findings.figures: Capital programme 2025-26 to 2029-30 detailed in Annex D; borrowing needed from end of 2026-27; internal or external method not yet determined
findings.quote: If the capital programme is delivered as per the current programme then borrowing may be needed towards the end of 2026/2027.

findings.paper_title: F.768 Full Council Report - Revenue and Capital Budget 2026_2027
findings.headline: New government business rates relief (Pubs and Music Venues) not included in budget due to late announcement
findings.detail: A new Pubs and Music Venues business rates relief was announced by government after the council had submitted its business rates estimates (NNDR1) to MHCLG. The council's budget numbers do not include any provision for this relief, and government has not yet provided details on how it will operate. This creates a potential unbudgeted cost if the council must forgo business rates income.
findings.matters: Late government announcements create budget management risk; if the relief is significant, the council could face unbudgeted income loss in a year when it is already projecting deficits and drawing on reserves.
findings.figures: Amount of potential impact not yet known; announced after NNDR1 submission
findings.quote: The budget numbers for the NNDR1 do not include anything around the new Pubs and Music Venues relief as this was announced after these forms had been processed and details are still to be received around how this relief would work.

findings.paper_title: F.768 Full Council Report - Revenue and Capital Budget 2026_2027
findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation costs between £1.5m and £2.2m, funding source reliability uncertain
findings.detail: The council faces a Local Government Reorganisation (LGR) programme in April 2028 with transition costs estimated at £1.5m to £2.2m depending on which government proposal is selected. The council proposes to fund this from its Business Rates Equalisation reserve. However, this reserve was established to cover future business rates fluctuations and may not be fully available if business rates volatility occurs during 2026-28.
findings.matters: Large one-off cost with uncertain scope and a funding source that could become unavailable; this represents a material unquantified future liability that could force unplanned reserve draws or service cuts.
findings.figures: LGR costs £1.5m to £2.2m; Business Rates Equalisation reserve is proposed funding source
findings.quote: It is expected that the funding for LGR for this Council will be between £1.5m and £2.2m depending on which proposal is selected.

findings.paper_title: F.768 Full Council Report - Revenue and Capital Budget 2026_2027
findings.headline: Council tax base growth significantly lower than projected, reducing expected income
findings.detail: The council's MTFS was based on an assumed tax base increase of 1.35% per annum. However, actual growth in 2025-2026 was only 0.97%, compared to the previous year's 1.98%. This sustained shortfall has forced the council to reduce the planning assumption to 1.25% per annum going forward, directly reducing expected council tax income from levels previously forecast.
findings.matters: Lower-than-expected tax base growth reduces a key revenue source and suggests either weaker housing development or higher than anticipated empty properties; lenders need visibility on whether growth assumptions are now realistic.
findings.figures: Tax base growth 2025-26: 0.97% (vs 1.98% prior year); MTFS assumption revised from 1.35% to 1.25% per annum
findings.quote: The MTFS was draft ed on a tax base increase of 1.3 5% per annum. At present, the increase in 2025/2026 is 0.97%, this was 1.98% for 2025/2026. The effect of this is to decrease in the council tax income from that previously expected. The current MTFS is based on a 1.25% increase per annum which has been reduced from the previous 1.35% due to the lower levels received in 2025/26.

findings.paper_title: F.768 Full Council Report - Revenue and Capital Budget 2026_2027
findings.headline: Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) grant from government remains uncertain beyond 2026-2027
findings.detail: The council is budgeting for EPR payments from DEFRA in 2026-2027 and has included this in the MTFS. However, government has explicitly advised this should not be seen as part of the settlement, and the council acknowledges significant uncertainty around EPR into the future. This creates forecast risk if the grant is withdrawn or reduced.
findings.matters: Material grant income with uncertain continuation creates planning risk; if withdrawn, the council would face an immediate budget adjustment in a year when reserves are already declining.
findings.figures: EPR payments included in 2026-27 budget and MTFS; amount not separately quantified
findings.quote: Accordingly, there is still uncertainty around EPR into the future however which needs to be considered in the future.

findings.paper_title: F.768 Full Council Report - Revenue and Capital Budget 2026_2027
findings.headline: Government funding reducing by £200k per year in cash terms over three-year settlement period with no inflation cover
findings.detail: Despite receiving a three-year settlement from government (which the council welcomed for planning certainty), the underlying core spending power is declining. Over the next three years, the council will face a cumulative reduction in cash terms of approximately £200k per year. This reduction does not account for inflationary pressures on contracts, pay, and services, making it 'increasingly more difficult to set a balanced budget into the future without the use of reserves or significant savings through service cuts.'
findings.matters: Real-terms funding reductions combined with inflation mean the council faces structural deficit pressure that cannot be solved through efficiency alone; a lender must assess whether proposed savings targets are achievable given these structural pressures.
findings.figures: £200k per year cash reduction over 3-year period; £0.0m to £6.0m (Fair Funding) in 2026-27; declining to £4.8m by 2028-29
findings.quote: this Council will see a reduction in cash terms over the next 3 years of around £200k per year (this can be seen in the table in 4.2) and obviously that does not cover any inflationary pressures that will be incurred over the period. Therefore, it will become increasingly more difficult to set a balanced budget into the future without the use of reserves or significant savings through service cuts.

findings.paper_title: F.768 Full Council Report - Revenue and Capital Budget 2026_2027
findings.headline: Publica partnership restructuring has created £600k unplanned cost burden with only partial savings recovery identified
findings.detail: The council's decision to pull services back from the Publica shared services partnership required a 'cost base reset' exercise that has taken years to complete. This has created an additional £600k burden on the 2026-2027 budget. The council has identified only £200k of a £230k targeted recovery from Publica savings, leaving £30k still to be found. A management group has been established to reduce the burden further during 2026-27, but the outcome is uncertain.
findings.matters: This shows material cost volatility in a major partnership and execution risk on cost reduction plans; a lender needs confidence that the council can manage complex shared services arrangements and deliver promised savings.
findings.figures: £600k additional cost; £230k targeted Publica savings; £200k already identified; £30k still unidentified
findings.quote: Additional pressure has been put onto the budget due to the resetting of Publica's Cost base which has been an exercise that has taken a number of years to properly conclude and introduce. This has created an additional burden on this Council of £600k and a group has been set up between Publica and FODDC management to reduce this additional cost as much as possible.

findings.paper_title: F.768 Full Council Report - Revenue and Capital Budget 2026_2027
findings.headline: Future Budget Deficit Reserve projected to be fully exhausted by end of 2027-2028
findings.detail: The council's key reserve for managing future deficits will be depleted within 18 months if spending continues at budgeted levels. Total reserves are forecast to fall from £12.6m in March 2026 to £10.4m in March 2027. The council explicitly warns that if action is not taken to correct the revenue deficit within the MTFS, reserves will fall below recommended minimum levels.
findings.matters: Depleted reserves reduce the council's financial resilience and ability to absorb unforeseen costs or revenue shocks; for lenders, this signals deteriorating financial flexibility and increased credit risk.
findings.figures: Reserves: £12.6m (Mar 2026) falling to £10.4m (Mar 2027); Budget Deficit Reserve £0.825m (Mar 2026); Minimum reserve threshold unspecified but implied as below £10.4m
findings.quote: Without taking action to correct the projected revenue deficit within the MTFS (Annex J), the Council will quickly find itself in a position where its reserves are depleted below recommended levels.

findings.paper_title: F.768 Full Council Report - Revenue and Capital Budget 2026_2027
findings.headline: Council projects inability to set a legal balanced budget by 2028-2029 without further identified savings
findings.detail: The council is already projecting a £3.327m funding gap over the planning period. The document explicitly states that without radical action to identify and deliver savings, the council will not be able to set a legal budget in 2028-2029 when the current three-year settlement ends. Current savings proposals for 2026-2027 total approximately £465k, but some are not yet fully identified (e.g., £50k transformation savings awaiting a March 2026 action plan).
findings.matters: A council unable to set a legal budget faces government intervention and reputational damage; lenders need assurance that the council has a credible path to financial sustainability.
findings.figures: £3.327m funding gap; 2026-27 savings £465k; Future Budget Deficit Reserve £0.825m; General fund balance £1.015m
findings.quote: Unless action is taken, the Council will be unable to set a legal budget in for 202 8-2029 (if required).

findings.headline: Council acknowledges insufficient funding to deliver all Net Zero 2030 climate action targets
findings.detail: The council has committed to achieving Net Zero 2030 as a corporate priority. However, it explicitly acknowledges that targets are ambitious and many long-term projects are challenging with insufficient funding available. Limited staff resource is also a constraint. This risk is scored 15 out of 25 (high).
findings.matters: Underfunded corporate commitments can create budget pressures later, or reputational damage and credibility loss if targets are not met, affecting the council's stability.
findings.figures: Risk score 15/25
findings.quote: Budget set aside for Action Plan however targets are ambitious and many projects can be longterm and challenging with insuffcient funding available.

findings.headline: Forest of Dean will cease to exist as a legal entity on 1 April 2028, merging into a new unitary authority
findings.detail: The government's English Devolution White Paper is facilitating amalgamation of two-tier councils into unitary authorities. The Gloucestershire councils' joint proposal was submitted to central government on 28 November 2025, with a decision expected in summer 2026. Forest of Dean will cease to exist as a separate council, with all services and employees transferring to the new unitary authority.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand that the council as a distinct borrowing entity will cease to exist in 2028, fundamentally affecting the nature and continuity of any medium-to-long-term lending relationship.
findings.figures: Vesting day 1 April 2028
findings.quote: The Glos Proposal has now been submitted to Central Government on 28/11/25 for their consideration and decision which is expected Summer 2026.

findings.headline: Reserves will be drawn down to fund Local Government Reorganization contributions
findings.detail: The government is facilitating local government reorganization for two-tier councils. All Gloucestershire councils submitted a joint proposal on 28 November 2025 (central government decision expected summer 2026). Forest of Dean will merge into a new unitary authority with a vesting day of 1 April 2028. The council expects to contribute to the LGR Glos budget and will need to use reserves for this.
findings.matters: Reserve drawdowns reduce the council's financial buffer for unexpected costs or emergencies, affecting overall financial resilience at a time of structural change.
findings.figures: Vesting day 1 April 2028; contribution amount not specified
findings.quote: There is also an expectation for FODDC to contribute towards the LGR Glos budget, which will need to be funded from reserves.

findings.headline: Publica service rebasing has increased costs by approximately £600k, with further significant increases expected for 2026/27
findings.detail: Following a Publica rebasing exercise, Forest of Dean's costs for services provided through Publica have increased by circa £600k in the current year. The council is now setting the budget for 2026/27 and expects a significant further increase in cost for FODDC. Work is underway to identify efficiency savings to offset these increases.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand how the council will absorb these cost increases through efficiency savings, and whether they will impact the budget position and require further action.
findings.figures: circa £600k cost increase materialized; significant additional increase budgeted for 26/27
findings.quote: following the Publica rebasing exercise, FODDC costs have increased by circa £600k. Work is underway to identify potential efficiency savings to bridge this gap.

news_drafts.headline: General Fund Balance remains at approximately £1.0m, providing only 1-2 weeks of operational cover.
news_drafts.lead: A general fund balance of £1m is insufficient to absorb service disruption, demand spikes, or delayed income. This leaves the council vulnerable to any unexpected expenditure and dependent on its earmarked reserves.
news_drafts.paper_title: F.789 Annex D - Reserves and General Balances 2025 26

news_drafts.headline: New District Council Initiatives reserve of £1.0m created in 2025/26, representing a significant new commitment or spending priority.
news_drafts.lead: A large reserve created in one year without prior provision suggests either new discretionary spending, new statutory obligations, or a strategic reallocation that lenders should understand in the context of the council's stated financial priorities.

news_drafts.headline: Council is drawing on Future Deficits Reserve, suggesting anticipated budget shortfalls.
news_drafts.lead: Depletion of a deficit-specific reserve demonstrates the council has already faced or is planning for funding gaps that could not be met from normal operations.
